clinicalPearls: Functional dyspepsia is chronic epigastric pain, burning, postprandial fullness, or early satiety without an identifiable structural cause on evaluation
It is subdivided into postprandial distress syndrome, dominated by meal-related fullness and early satiety, and epigastric pain syndrome
Diagnosis rests on symptom-based (Rome) criteria after appropriate exclusion of organic disease
Testing for and treating Helicobacter pylori benefits a subset of patients and is a recommended early step
Alarm features such as weight loss, bleeding, dysphagia, persistent vomiting, or older age at onset warrant endoscopy to exclude malignancy and ulcer
Acid suppression is a reasonable first-line therapy, with neuromodulators and prokinetics used for persistent symptoms
There is substantial overlap with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and irritable bowel syndrome, and psychological factors commonly modulate symptoms
reference.pathophysiology: Functional dyspepsia is a disorder of gut-brain interaction without structural disease. Contributing mechanisms include delayed gastric emptying, impaired fundic accommodation to a meal, visceral hypersensitivity to gastric distension and acid, low-grade duodenal inflammation and increased mucosal permeability, and altered central processing of visceral signals. Prior infection, Helicobacter pylori, psychological stress, and genetic predisposition can all contribute, producing symptoms disproportionate to any measurable physiological abnormality.
additionalDifferentials: Irritable bowel syndrome with upper gut overlap
additionalInvestigations: Helicobacter pylori testing (breath, stool antigen, or biopsy)
Upper endoscopy when alarm features are present or symptoms are refractory
Full blood count to screen for anaemia
Consideration of gastric emptying study when gastroparesis is suspected
Targeted biliary or pancreatic imaging when the history suggests these
redFlags: Persistent vomiting or a palpable epigastric mass
New dyspepsia in an older patient
reference.prognosis: Functional dyspepsia is a benign but often chronic and relapsing condition that can substantially impair quality of life; symptoms fluctuate over time and respond variably to treatment, but there is no increase in serious organic disease.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise and evaluate alarm features before labelling symptoms as functional
Repeated normal investigations without addressing the gut-brain nature of the disorder
Overlooking Helicobacter pylori as a treatable contributor
Escalating acid suppression indefinitely without considering neuromodulators or psychological factors
management: Test for and eradicate Helicobacter pylori with antibiotic-based combination therapy as an early step
Acid suppression with a proton pump inhibitor as first-line therapy, particularly for epigastric pain syndrome
Prokinetics for postprandial distress syndrome dominated by fullness and early satiety
Neuromodulators such as tricyclic antidepressants for persistent symptoms
Dietary and lifestyle advice with smaller low-fat meals, plus psychological therapies for refractory cases
Upper endoscopy to exclude ulcer and malignancy when alarm features or refractory symptoms are present
